2. The facts upon which the said Rule Nisi was issued, in short, are that on 18.11.89 Petrobangla, a statutory corporation, floated a tender inviting bids to carry line pipes, drilling materials etc. from Chittagong Port to various destinations. Six bidders including the petitioner and the respondent No. 4 participated in the bid which was opened on 30.11.89. The petitioner became lowest bidder. But the tender was cancelled and a fresh tender was floated on 24.12.89 violating the Rules contained in the Purchase Manual of Petrobangla relating to re-tender. However, this time 9 (nine) bidders including the petitioner and the respondent No. 4 participated and the tender was opened on 1.1.1990. This time also the petitioner became lowest bidder. The tender committee evaluated the bids on 3.1.1990 and recommended, as per Rule laid down in the Purchase Manual, to award the contract to the petitioner. The respondent No. 2 approved the said recommendation and forwarded to the respondent No. 1 Chairman of Petrobangla for final approval. In the meantime on 7.1.1990 the petitioner was asked to give the analysis of their offered price which they supplied on 8.1.90. The petitioner alleges that instead of awarding the contract to the petitioner, the respondent No. 1 on the one hand started secretly negotiating with the respondent No. 4 to reduce their price in an attempt to favour them unduly and on the other hand asked the Tender Committee to re-evaluate the bid of the petitioner. The Tender Committee accordingly re-evaluated the petitioner's bid and with intent to help the respondent No. 4 get the work, arbitrarily observed that the petitioners bid is technically non-responsive. Thereafter the respondent No. 3 passed the impugned letter of intent awarding the contract to the respondent No. 4 arbitrarily, malafide and in violation of the binding rules of their own Purchase Manual. Hence, the Writ. 

 6. Mr. Salauddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, attacked the impugned letter of intent awarding the contract to the respondent No. 4 on several grounds. Relying on the decision in the case of Sharping Matsajibi Samabaya Samity, 39 DLR (AD) 85, his first ground is that Petrobangla being an intrumentality of the Government is subject to the same constitutional and legal limitations as imposed under the Government and as such it cannot act arbitrarily but its actions must be in conformity with rational, relevant and non-discriminatory standard norms. Petrobangla as an instrumentality of the Government and being solely vested with the right to explore for petroleum and to deal with all operations connected therewith, framed guidelines and standard norms in the Purchase Manual for purchase and procurement of goods and services which are, according to its recital, binding upon Petrobangla. Mr. Salauddin referred to the various provisions of the said manual and submitted that the procedure and norms prescribed in the Purchase Manual regarding re-tender, evaluation and re-evaluation of bids, award of contract to the lowest bidder and award of contract by negotiation were not followed intentionally and the contract was awarded to the respondent No. 4 most arbitrarily and malafide. Hence the impugned letter of intent is liable to be set aside. 

 7. Mr. Salauddin's next ground is that the petitioner's bid has been rejected most arbitrarily on the manifestly erroneous premises that he was incapable of performing the contract. In so doing the respondents did not at all consider that the petitioner had successfully performed the largest and most difficult contracts in the past with the respondent. Mr. Salauddin then argued that the respondents negotiated with the respondent No. 4, allowed him to reduce his price and then awarded the contract to him behind the back of the petitioner and other bidders. This they have done mala fide and in the clear violation of rules contained in the Purchase Manual. To support his contention that Petrobangla being an instrumentality of the Government cannot act arbitrarily and that it must follow certain standard norms and guidelines in dealing with matters of awarding contracts and granting largess etc. to the citizen. Mr. Salauddin cited the decisions reported in AIR 1979 (SC) 1628, AIR 1986 (SC) 1527 and Sharping Matsajibis case reported in BLD 1987 (AD) 106 = 39 DLR (AD) 85. 

 9. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiya, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent No. 4 first of all submitted that neither there is any provision in Petroleum Act, 1974 for framing any Purchase Manual nor the same has been framed thereunder or any other law. So, the Purchase Manual, upon which the petitioner laid so much emphasis and based his case, has no statutory backing so as to make its violation remediable in Writ Jurisdiction. Mr. Bhuiyan further submits that since the Purchase Manual has not been framed under the authority of any law, it is a mere internal administrative instruction and the petitioner cannot invoke the aid of Article 102 of the Constitution against alleged violation of an internal administrative instruction which] has no statutory force at all. To support his contention Mr. Bhuiyan has cited the decisions reported in AIR 1965 (SC) 1196, AIR 1976 (SC) 1763, AIR 1981 (SC) 1368 and BLD 1981 (AD) 103. Mr. Bhuiyan has submitted further that although the Purchase Manual has no statutory force, yet no provision thereof has been violated in this case. In this connection Mr. Bhuiyan submitted that the respondent Nos. 1-3 had unfettered right to accept or reject any or all quotations without assigning any reason in terms of the provision of the tender documents itself and that neither the petitioner nor for that matter any of the bidders has any right to raise objection against such rejection. But in this case, he pointed out, the Tender Committee correctly evaluated the bids and the Board of Directors of Petrobangla after considering the evaluation report and other aspect of the matter decided in its meeting dated 8.1.1990 to award the contract in favour of the respondent No. 4 and in so doing the Board neither violated the rules of the Purchase Manual nor committed any illegality or infringed any legal right of the petitioner nor acted arbitrarily or malafide for collateral purpose which is to be alleged and proved in appropriate forum and cannot be decided in writ jurisdiction. Mr. Salauddin lastly submits that in re-evaluating the petitioners' bid the Tender Committee set up a criterion of the petitioner's ownership of vehicles required for the work which is per se discriminatory, firstly, because the tender document did not set up any such criterion of ownership of vehicles and secondly, they did not apply the same criterion for the petitioner and the respondent No. 4 inasmuch as the respondent No. 4 also did not own vehicles, yet their bid was not found non-responsive. This, be submits, is pure discriminatory and hence violative of Article 27 of the Constitution. We have checked the Tender documents and found that Clause 9 of the tender document clearly required of the bidders to give particulars of vehicles owned by them and to furnish certificate of ownership thereof. So, we do not find any substance in the arguments of Mr. Salauddin that the criterion of ownership of vehicles were per se discriminatory. 

 10. Apart from referring to the recitals of the Purchase Manual wherein it is stated that the same is binding for the Petrobangla, Mr. Salauddin could not place any materials before us to show that the Purchase Manual has been framed under the authority of any law or the same has otherwise acquired statutory force. Mr. Salauddin could not substantiate his argument that the petitioner's right has been impugned by the impugned work order. We are rather in agreement with the submission of Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan that Petrobangla has right in law as well as under the terms of the tender notice to reject the bid of the petitioner or for that matter any bid without assigning any reason although in this case good and sufficient reasons have been assigned as it was a case of choosing between the two bidders. The decisions cited by Mr. Salauddin Ahmed are not at all applicable in the facts and circumstances of the present case. So, we do not find any substance in the arguments advanced by Mr. Salauddin Ahmed.
